name: State of Goshen
label: boer states
description: The State of Goshen emerged on 24 October 1882 when Boer pastoralists led by Nicolaas Claudius Gey van Pittius established an autonomous settlement at Rooigrond on contested Tswana territory. Operating in defiance of British regional hegemony, the frontier republic maintained close ties with the neighbouring South African Republic and frequently engaged in local border skirmishes. On 6 August 1883, the polity agreed to unite with adjacent Stellaland, bringing an end to its brief period of standalone sovereignty. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Rooigrond; Common languages: Dutch and Tswana; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Republic; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 24 October 1882; Disestablished: 6 August 1883; Succeeded by: United States of Stellaland

name: Kingdom of Great Joseon
description: The Kingdom of Great Joseon experienced intensified imperial encroachment during the late nineteenth century, culminating in an era of substantial Qing Chinese political oversight following the military crisis of 1882. Governed from Hanseong by King Gojong, the kingdom strove to modernise its administrative apparatus while navigating competing pressures from Beijing and Tokyo. This phase of Chinese tributary tutelage formally unravelled in late 1894 when Japanese forces seized the royal palace during the First Sino-Japanese War. \n\n Status: Tributary protectorate of the Qing dynasty; Capital: Hanseong; Official languages: Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Neo-Confucianism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Late Joseon period; Reorganised: 1883; Disestablished: 24 October 1894; Succeeded by: Korean Empire

name: Kingdom of Langu
description: The Kingdom of Langu formed in 1883 as a breakaway Malay principality in the northern reaches of the Malayan Peninsula following internal dynastic disputes within the ruling house of Setul. Led by Tunku Muhammad, the breakaway realm maintained de facto local autonomy around its base in Langu for nearly a decade. The territory was subsequently reincorporated into neighbouring Siamese-influenced administrative structures during the regional consolidations of the early 1890s. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Langu; Common languages: Malay and Siamese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Imperial era; Established: 1883; Disestablished: 1891; Preceded by: Kingdom of Setul

name: Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla
description: Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla was established as an amalgamated British colonial dependency in 1883, bringing the islands of Saint Kitts, Nevis and Anguilla under a unified administration based at Basseterre. The Crown oversaw local governance and plantation agriculture while gradually expanding representative institutions through a shared legislative council. This administrative arrangement endured across the twentieth century until Anguilla formally broke away to remain a direct British overseas territory. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Basseterre; Official languages: English; Common languages: Saint Kitts Creole and Anguillian Creole; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Modern colonial era; Established: 1883; Disestablished: 1981; Succeeded by: Saint Kitts and Nevis

name: German South West Africa
description: German South West Africa was proclaimed in May 1883 when merchant Adolf Lüderitz acquired coastal land around Angra Pequena, inaugurating imperial Germany's first major colonial project in southern Africa. Administered successively from Otjimbingwe and Windhoek, colonial authorities displaced indigenous Herero and Nama communities to build a settler economy rooted in ranching and mining. Allied forces from the Union of South Africa overran the territory in July 1915, terminating German imperial governance. \n\n Status: Colony of the German Empire; Capital: Otjimbingwe and Windhoek; Official languages: German; Common languages: Khoekhoe, Herero, Oshiwambo and Afrikaans; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1 May 1883; Disestablished: 9 July 1915; Succeeded by: South West Africa

name: United States of Stellaland
label: boer states
description: The United States of Stellaland arose on 6 August 1883 through the administrative merger of the Republic of Stellaland and the neighbouring State of Goshen under Boer leadership at Vryburg. Commanded by Administrator Gerrit Jacobus van Niekerk, the fledgling republic sought to secure sovereign Boer control along vital trade corridors westward from the Transvaal. Mounting imperial pressure and British concern over Transvaal expansion prompted a military expedition under Sir Charles Warren, which dismantled the confederation in September 1884. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Vryburg; Common languages: Dutch and Tswana; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Federal republic; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 6 August 1883; Disestablished: 16 September 1884; Succeeded by: British Bechuanaland

name: Protectorate of Annam
description: The Protectorate of Annam was imposed by France upon the central provinces of Vietnam through the treaties of Hue signed in 1883 and 1884. Although the imperial court of the Nguyen dynasty remained seated at Hue, real administrative and fiscal authority rested with a resident-general appointed by Paris. In October 1887, the French colonial administration integrated Annam into the newly created Indochinese Union alongside Tonkin, Cochinchina and Cambodia. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Hue; Official languages: French, Vietnamese and Classical Chinese; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Indirect colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 25 August 1883; Disestablished: 17 October 1887; Succeeded by: Indochinese Union

name: Protectorate of Tonkin
description: The Protectorate of Tonkin took shape in August 1883 when French expeditionary forces compelled the court of Hue to cede administrative authority over northern Vietnam. Operating from Hanoi, French colonial officials gradually stripped imperial mandarins of executive power, implementing direct supervisory control over commerce and provincial taxation. In October 1887, French authorities incorporated Tonkin as a constituent territory within the newly established Indochinese Union. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Hanoi; Official languages: French, Vietnamese and Classical Chinese; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism, Confucianism and Folk religion; Government: Indirect colonial administration; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 25 August 1883; Disestablished: 17 October 1887; Succeeded by: Indochinese Union

name: British New Guinea
description: British New Guinea was established as an imperial protectorate in late 1883 before evolving into a formal Crown colony centred at Port Moresby. Prompted by urgent requests from Queensland and other Australian colonies wary of German expansion in the Pacific, the British administration managed coastal trade, judicial affairs and relations with indigenous Papuan societies. In March 1902, the British government transferred administrative responsibility for the territory to the newly formed Commonwealth of Australia. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Port Moresby; Official languages: English; Common languages: Motu, Hiri Motu and Papuan languages; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 6 November 1883; Disestablished: 18 March 1902; Succeeded by: Territory of Papua

name: French Dahomey
description: French Dahomey originated as a colonial holding in 1884 when French authorities consolidated coastal trading enclaves and treaties around Porto-Novo to counter British commercial dominance. Following intense military campaigns against the Kingdom of Dahomey in the early 1890s, French forces deposed King Behanzin and annexed the hinterland into French West Africa. Porto-Novo served as the colonial capital until the territory attained self-government within the French Community in December 1958. \n\n Status: Colony of France; Capital: Porto-Novo; Official languages: French; Common languages: Fon, Yoruba and Bariba; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1884; Disestablished: 11 December 1958; Succeeded by: Republic of Dahomey

name: Sultanate of Ujiji
label: arab polities of east congo
description: The Sultanate of Ujiji flourished along the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika as a prominent Arab-Swahili mercantile stronghold governed by local liwalis and trading magnates. By 1884, the territory fell under the de facto dominance of the trader Rumaliza, who utilised Ujiji as a regional base for lucrative ivory caravans and slave trading networks across eastern Congo. German colonial forces subsequently asserted imperial authority over the lake region in July 1890, extinguishing the autonomous sultanate. \n\n Status: Autonomous sultanate under mercantile hegemony; Capital: Ujiji; Common languages: Swahili and Manyema; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Mercantile sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1884; Disestablished: 1 July 1890; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: District of Alaska
description: The District of Alaska was created by the United States Congress through the First Organic Act of 17 May 1884, establishing civil government over the vast northern territory following seventeen years of military oversight. Initially administered from Sitka and later from Juneau after 1906, the district witnessed rapid population growth and infrastructural development during the Klondike Gold Rush. This transitional administrative regime concluded on 24 August 1912 when Congress formally reorganised the region as an incorporated territory. \n\n Status: Unincorporated territory of the United States; Capital: Sitka and Juneau; Official languages: English; Common languages: Tlingit, Yupik, Inupiaq and Russian; Government: Civil territorial administration; Historical era: American territorial expansion; Established: 17 May 1884; Disestablished: 24 August 1912; Succeeded by: Territory of Alaska

name: German Togoland
description: German Togoland was founded in July 1884 when imperial envoy Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty of protection with Mlapa III, the ruler of Togo-Be on the Gulf of Guinea. Initially administered from coastal stations at Bagida and Sebe, the colonial government relocated its headquarters to Lome in 1897 while systematically extending transport links into the agricultural interior. At the outbreak of the First World War in August 1914, Anglo-French expeditionary forces invaded and compelled the German garrison to capitulate. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the German Empire; Capital: Bagida, Sebe and Lome; Official languages: German; Common languages: Ewe, Kotokoli and Kabye; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 5 July 1884; Disestablished: 26 August 1914; Succeeded by: British Togoland and French Togoland

name: German Cameroon
description: German Cameroon was proclaimed in July 1884 when treaties negotiated with Duala chiefs established an imperial protectorate over the coastal lagoons of the Bight of Biafra. Administered successively from Douala, Buea and Yaounde, the colonial apparatus pursued aggressive military expansion inland, subverting local fondoms and lamidates to establish sprawling rubber and cocoa plantations. Combined British, French and Belgian forces overran the colony during the First World War, concluding German rule in March 1916. \n\n Status: Colony of the German Empire; Capital: Douala, Buea and Yaounde; Official languages: German; Common languages: Duala, Beti, Basaa, Fula and Hausa; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 14 July 1884; Disestablished: 4 March 1916; Succeeded by: French Cameroon and British Cameroons

name: Mambila
description: The Mambila polity encompasses the autonomous precolonial chieftaincies situated across the rugged Mambilla Plateau and adjacent Ndòm plains along the present-day Nigeria-Cameroon frontier. Governed through kin-based lineages and village elders, the highland communities fiercely defended their farming settlements and livestock against Fulani slave raiders from the neighbouring Adamawa Emirate. Independent local governance endured until the opening years of the twentieth century, when German and British colonial expeditions partitioned the plateau. \n\n Status: Autonomous tribal chieftaincy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Mambila dialects; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 22 July 1884; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Cameroon and Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: New Republic
label: boer states
description: The New Republic was founded on 5 August 1884 by Boer irregulars who had aided Dinuzulu kaCetshwayo in his successful bid for the Zulu royal throne in exchange for substantial territorial grants. Establishing their capital at Vryheid, the settlers drafted a republican constitution and selected Lucas Johannes Meyer as president. Hemmed in by British colonial encirclement in Natal, the fledgling republic voluntarily petitioned for annexation by the South African Republic, formally dissolving in July 1888. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Vryheid; Common languages: Dutch and Zulu; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Presidential republic; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 5 August 1884; Disestablished: 20 July 1888; Succeeded by: South African Republic

name: Republic of Peru
description: The Republic of Peru encountered widespread social upheaval between September 1884 and December 1885 when an indigenous peasant rebellion led by Pedro Pablo Atusparia seized control of the Callejón de Huaylas in the department of Ancash. Sparked by onerous personal tribute levies and arbitrary governance following the devastating War of the Pacific, the insurgents established regional rebel authority across Huaraz and surrounding highland valleys. National government forces gradually reasserted central control through decisive military counter-offensives late in 1885. \n\n Status: Revolutionary rebel administration; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Official languages: Spanish and Quechua; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Peasant provisional regime; Historical era: Postwar reconstruction; Established: 1 September 1884; Disestablished: 3 December 1885; Succeeded by: Republic of Peru

name: German New Guinea
description: German New Guinea was established in November 1884 when imperial naval expeditions declared protectorates over Kaiser-Wilhelmsland in north-eastern New Guinea and the adjacent Bismarck Archipelago. Administered successively from Finschhafen, Herbertshöhe and Rabaul, the colonial authority supported commercial copra plantations operated by the German New Guinea Company before transitioning to direct imperial governance. Australian expeditionary forces occupied the territory shortly after the outbreak of the First World War in late 1914. \n\n Status: Colony of the German Empire; Capital: Finschhafen, Herbertshöhe and Rabaul; Official languages: German; Common languages: Unserdeutsch, Tolai and Papuan languages; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Imperial expansion; Established: 4 November 1884; Disestablished: 14 November 1914; Succeeded by: Territory of New Guinea

name: Santa Lucia Bay
description: Santa Lucia Bay emerged as a short-lived German colonial enterprise on the Zululand coast in November 1884 when agents representing merchant Adolf Lüderitz concluded concession treaties with local Zulu authorities. The trading venture sought imperial recognition to anchor German commercial access along the south-eastern African seaboard. Strong British diplomatic protests invoking prior maritime treaties forced Berlin to renounce all territorial claims in May 1885, leaving the inlet under undisputed British paramountcy. \n\n Status: Colonial commercial enclave; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, Zulu and English; Religion: Christianity and Traditional beliefs; Government: Chartered trading agency; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 19 November 1884; Disestablished: 7 May 1885; Succeeded by: British Zululand

name: Oil Rivers Protectorate
description: The Oil Rivers Protectorate was instituted by Great Britain in December 1884 across the coastal delta and river basins of eastern Nigeria to safeguard British mercantile supremacy in the palm oil trade. Operating from consular headquarters at Old Calabar, British officials managed commercial relations with indigenous city-states while enforcing maritime trade regulations along navigable waterways. In May 1893, imperial authorities reorganised and expanded the dependency, officially redesignating it as the Niger Coast Protectorate. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Old Calabar; Official languages: English; Common languages: Efik, Ibibio, Igbo and Ijaw; Government: Consular administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 19 December 1884; Disestablished: 12 May 1893; Succeeded by: Niger Coast Protectorate

name: German East Africa Company
description: The German East Africa Company originated under the leadership of Carl Peters, who secured extensive land treaties across modern Tanzania through the Society for German Colonisation. In early 1885, the company established an operational base at Bagamoyo and received an imperial charter conferring extensive sovereign rights over trade and administration. On 27 February 1885, the imperial government placed these private holdings under formal state protection, laying the foundation for direct German colonial governance in East Africa. \n\n Status: Chartered company administration; Capital: Bagamoyo; Official languages: German; Common languages: Swahili; Government: Commercial company rule; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1885; Disestablished: 27 February 1885; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: International Association of the Congo
description: The International Association of the Congo was founded in November 1879 by King Leopold II of Belgium as a private commercial vehicle to establish control over the Congo River basin. Headquartered at Boma, the association concluded hundreds of treaties with local African rulers and secured international recognition at the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885. On 1 August 1885, Leopold formally transformed the association's territorial claims into the Congo Free State, placing the region under his personal autocratic rule. \n\n Status: Commercial holding association in personal union; Capital: Boma; Official languages: French; Common languages: Lingala, Kikongo and Swahili; Government: Absolute corporate monarchy; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1885; Disestablished: 1 August 1885; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Kapitaï and Koba
description: Kapitaï and Koba comprised two coastal enclaves between the Pongo and Dubreka rivers in present-day Guinea where German commercial agents secured local treaties in early 1885. Financed through the Württembergische Vereinsbank, the enterprise attempted to develop an imperial foothold known colloquially as Colinsland to monopolise riverine trade. French diplomatic opposition resulted in the Franco-German Protocol of 24 December 1885, by which Germany relinquished all rights in the Dubreka region in exchange for French concessions elsewhere in West Africa. \n\n Status: Colonial enclave of the German Empire; Capital: Dubreka; Official languages: German; Common languages: Baga and Susu; Government: Colonial agency; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1885; Disestablished: 24 December 1885; Succeeded by: French Guinea

name: Kingdom of Aneho
description: The Kingdom of Aneho functioned as an influential Mina coastal principality situated on the Gulf of Guinea between Lake Togo and the Atlantic Ocean. In 1885, French colonial authorities briefly occupied the town of Aneho, then known as Little Popo, to counter German advances along the Slave Coast. Under the Franco-German border convention concluded on 24 December 1885, France transferred its claim over Aneho to Germany, which promptly absorbed the coastal polity into German Togoland. \n\n Status: Occupied coastal kingdom; Capital: Aneho; Common languages: Gen and French; Religion: Traditional African religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy under military occupation; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1885; Disestablished: 24 December 1885; Succeeded by: German Togoland

name: Zheltuga Republic
description: The Zheltuga Republic was an unauthorised proto-state established in 1885 along the Zheltuga River in the Amur River basin by thousands of Russian and Chinese gold prospectors. Known informally as California on the Amur, the polyglot mining encampment elected Karl Fassi as president and maintained an orderly code of frontier law with its own militia and courts. Qing imperial authorities viewed the enclave as an unacceptable violation of Chinese territorial sovereignty, dispatching troops who dispersed the settlement in February 1886. \n\n Status: Unrecognised proto-state; Capital: Zheltuga; Common languages: Russian and Mandarin Chinese; Government: Frontier mining republic; Historical era: Late Qing period; Established: 1885; Disestablished: 1 February 1886; Succeeded by: Qing dynasty

name: Portuguese Congo
description: Portuguese Congo was established on 1 February 1885 following the conclusion of the Treaty of Simulambuco, in which the local princes of the Ngoyo kingdom placed the coastal enclave of Cabinda under Portuguese Crown protection. Governed from Cabinda, the protectorate maintained separate administrative status from Portuguese West Africa while securing Portuguese commercial navigation near the mouth of the Congo River. This autonomous protectorate structure remained in force until 1933, when Portugal consolidated Cabinda directly into the colonial administration of Angola. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Portugal; Capital: Cabinda; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Kikongo and Fiote; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial protectorate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1 February 1885; Disestablished: 1933; Succeeded by: Portuguese Angola

name: German East Africa
description: German East Africa was proclaimed on 27 February 1885 when the German Empire assumed sovereign responsibility over the vast East African territories claimed by the German East Africa Company. Administered from coastal Bagamoyo and subsequently from Dar es Salaam, imperial forces brutally suppressed regional resistance, including the coastal Abushiri revolt and the widespread Maji Maji rebellion. German colonial governance collapsed in November 1918 following imperial defeat in the First World War, after which the League of Nations partitioned the colony between Britain and Belgium. \n\n Status: Colony of the German Empire; Capital: Bagamoyo and Dar es Salaam; Official languages: German; Common languages: Swahili, Arabic, Kirundi and Kinyarwanda; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 27 February 1885; Disestablished: 25 November 1918; Succeeded by: Tanganyika Territory and Ruanda-Urundi

name: Bechuanaland Protectorate
description: The Bechuanaland Protectorate was established on 23 March 1885 when Great Britain proclaimed sovereign protection over the northern Tswana territories extending north of the Molopo River. Governed for decades from the extraterritorial administrative seat of Mafeking in the Cape Colony, imperial authorities preserved indigenous chiefly authority while thwarting territorial annexation by Boer republics and Cecil Rhodes's chartered company. The protectorate preserved its distinct territorial integrity until achieving full independence as the Republic of Botswana on 30 September 1966. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Mafeking; Official languages: English; Common languages: Setswana and Kalanga; Government: Imperial protectorate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 23 March 1885; Disestablished: 30 September 1966; Succeeded by: Republic of Botswana

name: German Witu Company
description: The German Witu Company assumed administrative responsibility over the coastal Swahili sultanate of Witu in April 1885 through private concessions secured by the Denhardt brothers. Operating from Witu near the mouth of the Tana River, the commercial entity sought to construct a fortified trading monopoly in timber and agriculture along the Lamu coast. Imperial Germany formalised these corporate concessions on 27 May 1885, replacing direct commercial company rule with an official imperial protectorate over the territory. \n\n Status: Chartered commercial enclave; Capital: Witu; Official languages: German; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Government: Commercial company administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 8 April 1885; Disestablished: 27 May 1885; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Witu

name: Genyigba
description: Genyigba was a traditional coastal chieftaincy situated around Grand-Popo in south-western modern Benin along the Bight of Benin. Facing encroaching German territorial ambitions from neighbouring Aneho, local leaders concluded a treaty of protection with French colonial representatives on 17 April 1885. This arrangement preserved local municipal autonomy under French naval oversight until October 1886, when French authorities absorbed the coastal chieftaincy into the expanding administrative boundaries of French West African possessions. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Grand-Popo; Official languages: French; Common languages: Gen and Fon; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Coastal chieftaincy; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 17 April 1885; Disestablished: 26 October 1886; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Sultanate of Witu
description: The Sultanate of Witu, also known as Wituland, became an imperial German protectorate on 27 May 1885 following formal diplomatic agreements between Sultan Ahmad ibn Fumo Bakari and imperial German representatives. Centred on the fortified town of Witu north of the Tana River delta, the sultanate provided Germany with a strategic foothold on the East African coast to counterbalance British influence in Zanzibar. Under the Anglo-German Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of 1 July 1890, Germany ceded its protectorate over Witu to Great Britain. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the German Empire; Capital: Witu; Official languages: German and Arabic; Common languages: Swahili; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 27 May 1885; Disestablished: 1 July 1890; Succeeded by: British East Africa Protectorate

name: Congo Free State
description: The Congo Free State was established on 1 August 1885 as a sovereign absolute monarchy held in personal union by King Leopold II of Belgium. Administered from Boma and directed entirely from Brussels, the Free State operated through the Force Publique to extract immense wealth in ivory and wild rubber through brutal systems of forced labour. Escalating international outrage over widespread atrocities and devastating population decline compelled the Belgian Parliament to annex the territory as the Belgian Congo in November 1908. \n\n Status: Sovereign state in personal union with the King of the Belgians; Capital: Boma; Official languages: French; Common languages: Lingala, Kikongo, Swahili and Tshiluba; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Absolute personal monarchy; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1 August 1885; Disestablished: 15 November 1908; Succeeded by: Belgian Congo

name: British Bechuanaland
description: British Bechuanaland was formally constituted as a British Crown colony on 30 September 1885, encompassing the territory situated south of the Molopo River between the Transvaal and the Kalahari Desert. Administered from Vryburg, the colony was established following Sir Charles Warren's military expedition, which dismantled the Boer republics of Stellaland and Goshen. The colonial administration supervised European ranching settlement and Tswana reserves until 16 November 1895, when the entire territory was incorporated into the Cape Colony. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Vryburg; Official languages: English; Common languages: Setswana, Dutch and Afrikaans; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 30 September 1885; Disestablished: 16 November 1895; Succeeded by: Cape Colony

name: Republic of Upingtonia
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Upingtonia was founded on 20 October 1885 by Trekboers led by George Diederik P. Prinsloo on land purchased from Ovambo chief Kambonde in north-central Namibia. Centred at Grootfontein, the fledgling settler republic was initially named in honour of Cape Prime Minister Thomas Upington in an unsuccessful bid to gain British protection. Renamed Lijdensrust in 1887, the beleaguered settlement suffered endemic tribal warfare and internal collapse before being absorbed into German South West Africa. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Grootfontein; Common languages: Dutch, Afrikaans and Oshiwambo; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Presidential republic; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 20 October 1885; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Kingdom of Serbia (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Serbia conducted wartime military administrations across occupied territories beyond its pre-war frontiers during regional conflicts in late 1885, the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 and the First World War. Operating without a permanent municipal seat, Serbian army commanders exercised civil and martial jurisdiction over occupied sectors of Bulgaria, Kosovo, the Sandzak and Vardar Macedonia. These transitional occupation zones functioned until formal peace treaties, military retreats or post-war international settlements established permanent political boundaries. \n\n Status: Military occupation administration; Administrative seat: Mobile field command; Official languages: Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Balkan conflicts and World War I; Established: 17 November 1885; Disestablished: 11 February 1916; Preceded by: Ottoman Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Serbia

name: Bulgaria (Military Occupation)
description: Bulgaria maintained military occupation regimes across disputed territories during the Serbo-Bulgarian War of 1885, the Balkan Wars, the First World War and the Second World War. Administered by royal armed forces command rather than a settled capital, the occupying authorities oversaw logistical transport, civil security and resource extraction in parts of eastern Serbia, Macedonia and Western Thrace. These temporary occupational arrangements were repeatedly overturned by military defeats, diplomatic treaties and the conclusion of worldwide hostilities. \n\n Status: Military occupation administration; Administrative seat: Mobile army headquarters; Official languages: Bulgarian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Military occupation command; Historical era: Balkan conflicts and World Wars; Established: 27 November 1885; Disestablished: 1 June 1945; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Yugoslavia and Kingdom of Greece

name: Sultanate of Johor
label: unfederated malay states
description: The Sultanate of Johor became an unfederated protected state of the British Empire on 11 December 1885 when Sultan Abu Bakar negotiated a landmark treaty of friendship with London. Governed from Johor Bahru, the sultan modernised the state's legal code, bureaucracy and infrastructure while encouraging large-scale commercial cultivation of gambier, pepper and rubber. Johor maintained considerable internal autonomy under British imperial protection until the Japanese invasion of Malaya swept through the peninsula in early 1942. \n\n Status: British protected state; Capital: Johor Bahru; Official languages: Malay; Common languages: English and Chinese dialects; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Malaya; Established: 11 December 1885; Disestablished: 31 January 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese occupation of Malaya

name: Chitral State
label: indian princely states
description: Chitral State was an autonomous mountain kingdom nestled within the high valleys of the Hindu Kush that entered into formal alliance with the British Raj in 1886. Ruled by hereditary monarchs bearing the title of Mehtar from the capital of Chitral, the state occupied an invaluable strategic position along the northern frontier of British India near the Pamirs and Afghanistan. British political agents supervised defence and foreign policy while preserving traditional dynastic governance until the partition of India in August 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state of the British Raj; Capital: Chitral; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Khowar, Pashto and Shina; Religion: Sunni Islam and Ismaili Islam; Government: Autocratic princely monarchy; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 14 August 1947; Succeeded by: Dominion of Pakistan

name: Hopong State
label: shan states
description: Hopong State was a constituent Shan principality located in the Central Division of the Southern Shan States that came under British imperial paramountcy in 1886 following the annexation of Upper Burma. Centred on the town of Hopong in the fertile Nam Pawn basin, the state was ruled by a hereditary local prince known as a myoza. The British administration oversaw tribute and regional security while preserving native customary rule until Burmese independence in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Hopong; Common languages: Shan, Pa-O and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Princely state monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: Hsamonghkam State
label: shan states
description: Hsamonghkam State, historically known as Thamaingkan, was a prominent Shan principality situated in the Myelat division of the Southern Shan States that accepted British suzerainty in 1886. Governed by a hereditary myoza from its administrative seat at Aungpan, the state encompassed important trade routes connecting the Shan plateau to central Burma. British authorities integrated the principality into the Federated Shan States in 1922, maintaining indirect rule until the transfer of sovereign power to Burma in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Aungpan; Common languages: Shan, Danu and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Princely state monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: Hsatung State
label: shan states
description: Hsatung State, also known as Thaton, was a traditional Shan principality in the Nam Pawn valley that came under British imperial oversight in 1886 following the collapse of the Konbaung dynasty. Administered from its capital at Hsihseng, the state possessed a predominantly Pa-O population ruled by a hereditary Shan myoza. British authorities supervised foreign relations and regional peace while preserving indigenous judicial customs until the termination of colonial rule in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Hsihseng; Common languages: Pa-O, Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Princely state monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: Hsawnghsup State
label: shan states
description: Hsawnghsup State, known to the Burmese as Thaungdut, was an outlying Shan principality situated along the western banks of the Chindwin River near the frontier of Manipur. British imperial authorities confirmed the state's protected princely status in 1886, recognising its hereditary saopha as ruler over extensive teak forests and river trading settlements. The enclave retained distinct local administrative autonomy within British Burma until its integration into the newly independent Union of Burma in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Thaungdut; Common languages: Shan, Manipuri and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Princely state monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma
