Inhabited by the Austroasiatic-speaking Wa people, the region lacked centralised urban capitals and was defended by fortified hill villages against external incursions. British authorities asserted nominal protectorate suzerainty over the borderland in 1886, maintaining minimal administrative interference until border demarcations with Qing China were initiated in 1895. \n\n Status: Protected tribal confederation; Capital: Pangkham; Common languages: Wa, Shan and Southwestern Mandarin; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Decentralised tribal chieftaincies; Historical era: Imperial frontier era; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 1895; Succeeded by: British Burma and Qing dynasty

name: Wanyin State
label: shan states
description: Wanyin State, known in Burmese as Banyin, was a compact Shan principality in the Central Division of the Southern Shan States situated south-east of Taunggyi. Seated at the town of Banyin, the local myoza directed agricultural cultivation across fertile upland valleys and managed local market commerce. British imperial authorities confirmed the state's protected princely status in 1886, supervising regional peace and revenue until the transfer of sovereign powers to Burma in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Banyin; Common languages: Shan, Pa-O and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Princely state monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: Wuntho State
label: shan states
description: Wuntho State was a historic Shan principality situated in Upper Burma between the Irrawaddy and Chindwin rivers, encompassing extensive teak forests and alluvial plains. Governed from the fortified town of Wuntho, the hereditary sawbwa resisted increasing colonial encroachment following the initial British declaration of paramountcy in 1886. In 1891, the sawbwa launched an armed rebellion against imperial forces, leading to the military conquest of Wuntho and its subsequent reduction to a regular British district. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Wuntho; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary sawbwa monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Yawnghwe State
label: shan states
description: Yawnghwe State was the pre-eminent principality of the Southern Shan States, encompassing the fertile plains surrounding Inle Lake and the mountain ranges beyond. Seated at his royal palace in Nyaungshwe, the influential saopha governed vibrant communities of Intha, Shan and Danu peoples while the British superintendent maintained headquarters nearby at Taunggyi. British protection was formalised in 1886, preserving dynastic rule until the state's accession to the newly independent Union of Burma in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Nyaungshwe; Common languages: Shan, Intha, Danu and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary saopha monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: Yengan State
label: shan states
description: Yengan State, historically known as Ywangan, was a rugged principality in the Myelat Division of the Southern Shan States. Centred on the village of Yengan in the Zawgyi river basin, the domain was populated predominantly by Danu farmers alongside Shan and Pa-O minorities. British colonial authorities brought the state under imperial protection in 1886, preserving traditional leadership under local ngwegunhmus until the transfer of power to independent Burma in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Yengan; Common languages: Danu, Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1886; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: Gilbert and Ellice Islands
description: The Gilbert and Ellice Islands formed a vast British Pacific protectorate established following the Anglo-German Declaration of April 1886, which demarcated imperial spheres of influence across the central Pacific. Administered through a resident commissioner headquartered at Bairiki on Tarawa, the territory linked the Micronesian Gilbert archipelago with the Polynesian Ellice Islands. The British colonial administration governed copra cultivation and island shipping until the two groups peacefully separated into modern Tuvalu and Kiribati in the 1970s. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Bairiki; Official languages: English; Common languages: Gilbertese and Tuvaluan; Government: British colonial residency; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 6 April 1886; Disestablished: 1976; Succeeded by: Gilbert Islands and Tuvalu

name: Kingdom of Nauru
description: The Kingdom of Nauru was brought into the German imperial sphere of influence on 6 April 1886 under the terms of the Anglo-German Partition of the Western Pacific. Centred administratively at Yaren, the isolated phosphate-rich island was governed through indigenous clan chiefs under the supervision of the German imperial commissioner based in the Marshall Islands. Direct German military annexation followed in 1888, bringing an end to the prolonged Nauruan Tribal War and extinguishing the island's traditional sovereign autonomy. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the German Empire; Capital: Yaren; Official languages: German; Common languages: Nauruan; Religion: Traditional animism and Christianity; Government: Traditional chieftaincy under imperial protection; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 6 April 1886; Disestablished: 1889; Succeeded by: German New Guinea

name: Republic of Independent Guiana
description: The Republic of Independent Guiana, commonly known as Counani, was proclaimed on 20 July 1886 in the disputed territory between French Guiana and the Empire of Brazil. Led by French journalist Jules Gros from the settlement of Counani, the unrecognised regime claimed a vast tract of Amazonian rainforest populated by native Amerindians, Quilombola communities and European adventurers. The self-declared republic collapsed by 1892 as diplomatic agreements between France and Brazil clarified regional borders and dispersed the filibuster administration. \n\n Status: Unrecognised presidential republic; Capital: Counani; Official languages: French; Common languages: Portuguese and Guyanese Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional presidential republic; Historical era: Late nineteenth century; Established: 20 July 1886; Disestablished: 1892; Succeeded by: French Guiana and Republic of Brazil

name: Republic of Colombia
description: The Republic of Colombia was inaugurated on 8 August 1886 with the adoption of a centralist constitution engineered by President Rafael Núñez, replacing the decentralised United States of Colombia. Seated at Bogotá, the state consolidated executive power, restored the pre-eminent role of the Roman Catholic Church and transformed former sovereign states into administrative departments. This unitary constitutional structure survived recurring political conflicts, including the Thousand Days' War, and forms the institutional basis of the modern nation. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: Bogotá; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: Congress of Colombia; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 8 August 1886; Preceded by: United States of Colombia; Currency: Colombian peso

name: Emirate of Adrar
description: The Emirate of Adrar was a prominent Saharan nomadic realm centred on the oasis town of Atar in modern Mauritania that entered into protection treaties with Spain in 1887. Ruled by the hereditary Hassaniya emir of the Oulad Qaylan and Oulad Ammoni, the polity controlled trans-Saharan caravan routes connecting the Senegal River basin to Morocco. Spanish administrative presence remained nominal, and French colonial expeditions gradually overran the territory in January 1909, incorporating Adrar into French West Africa. \n\n Status: Protectorate claimed by Spain; Capital: Atar; Common languages: Hassaniya Arabic and Berber dialects; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional emirate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1887; Disestablished: 9 January 1909; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Little Free State
label: boer states
description: The Little Free State, known in Afrikaans as Klein Vrystaat, was established in 1887 by Boer settlers on land ceded by Swazi king Mbandzeni near the modern town of Piet Retief. Governed from Vaalkop Farm by an elected triumvirate headed by J.J. Bezuidenhout, the miniature pastoral republic sought to secure independent grazing lands free from British colonial intervention. Unable to sustain diplomatic viability, the settler community requested integration into the South African Republic, formally dissolving on 2 August 1891. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Piet Retief; Common languages: Dutch and Afrikaans; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Triumvirate republic; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1887; Disestablished: 2 August 1891; Succeeded by: South African Republic

name: Republic of Lijdensrust
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Lijdensrust was proclaimed in 1887 as the reorganised continuation of the short-lived Boer state of Upingtonia in northern Namibia. Centred at Grootfontein, the settler community struggled against persistent isolation, internal factionalism and hostile clashes with local Ovambo and San populations. Lacking formal diplomatic backing from either Britain or the Transvaal, the beleaguered republic ceased operations in July 1887 when imperial German forces absorbed the settlement into German South West Africa. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Grootfontein; Common languages: Dutch and Afrikaans; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Presidential republic; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1887; Disestablished: 1 July 1887; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Sultanate of Mwali
label: comoros sultanates;polities of the swahili coast
description: The Sultanate of Mwali, also known as Mohéli, accepted French imperial protection in 1887 following the signing of formal conventions between local dynastic authorities and French naval representatives. Governed from the coastal capital of Fomboni, the island realm maintained traditional maritime commerce and vanilla cultivation across the Mozambique Channel. French colonial authorities gradually curtailed the autonomy of the sultanate before formally abolishing the monarchy in 1922 to integrate Mohéli into the Colony of Madagascar and Dependencies. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Fomboni; Common languages: Comorian, French and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional Islamic sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1887; Disestablished: 1922; Succeeded by: French Madagascar

name: Sultanate of Ndzuwani
label: comoros sultanates;polities of the swahili coast
description: The Sultanate of Ndzuwani, historically referred to by European navigators as Anjouan, was placed under French colonial protection in 1887 after Sultan Abdallah III entered into formal agreements with Paris. Seated at the historic fortified port of Mutsamudu, the island polity was renowned for its deepwater anchorages, sugar plantations and trading networks across the Comoro archipelago. French colonial administrators steadily centralised fiscal control, culminating in the formal annexation of Ndzuwani as a direct French possession in 1922. \n\n Status: Colony and protectorate of France; Capital: Mutsamudu; Common languages: Comorian, French and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate under colonial administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1887; Disestablished: 1922; Succeeded by: French Madagascar

name: Sultanate of Ngazidja
label: comoros sultanates;polities of the swahili coast
description: The Sultanate of Ngazidja was formed on the island of Grande Comore in 1887 when Sultan Said Ali bin Said Omar of Bambao unified rival insular chieftaincies into a centralised realm. Operating from the administrative capital of Moroni, the sultan sought French diplomatic backing to consolidate his fragile paramountcy over competing local notables. While formally maintaining sovereign status, the polity functioned under extensive French colonial influence until France formally annexed Grande Comore alongside the other Comoro islands in 1922. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate under French influence; Capital: Moroni; Common languages: Comorian, Arabic and French; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Centralised Islamic sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1887; Disestablished: 1922; Succeeded by: French Madagascar

name: Sultanate of Utetera
label: arab polities of east congo
description: The Sultanate of Utetera was an expansive Arab-Swahili mercantile state established across the upper Congo and Maniema regions by merchant Hamad bin Muhammad el Murjebi, known as Tippu Tip. Governed from the fortified trading emporium of Kasongo, the sultanate commanded extensive riverine ivory networks and armed caravans stretching to Lake Tanganyika. Despite nominal appointment as a provincial governor for the Congo Free State in 1887, Tippu Tip operated independently until Belgian colonial forces crushed his forces in October 1893 during the Congo Arab War. \n\n Status: Sovereign mercantile sultanate; Capital: Kasongo; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Mercantile autocracy; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 24 February 1887; Disestablished: 20 October 1893; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Kingdom of 'Uvea
description: The Kingdom of 'Uvea was a traditional Polynesian chiefdom occupying the island of Wallis in the South Pacific that entered into French protection on 5 April 1887. Following a treaty signed by Queen Amelia Tokagahahau Aliki, the island preserved indigenous customary laws, Catholic missionary influence and the traditional paramount chieftaincy at Mata-Utu. In March 1888, French authorities formalised regional administrative arrangements by integrating 'Uvea into the unified Protectorate of Wallis and Futuna under the governor of New Caledonia. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Mata-Utu; Official languages: French; Common languages: Wallisian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Customary Polynesian monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 5 April 1887; Disestablished: 5 March 1888; Succeeded by: Wallis and Futuna Protectorate

name: Imperial British East Africa Company
description: The Imperial British East Africa Company was founded by merchant William Mackinnon to exploit commercial concessions and assert British imperial control over eastern Africa. Operating from the port of Mombasa, the chartered corporation concluded treaties with indigenous leaders, established interior trading posts and laid early transport infrastructure across modern Kenya and Uganda. Chronic financial insolvency and escalating administrative costs forced the company to surrender its royal charter in July 1895, transferring its territories to direct Crown rule as the East Africa Protectorate. \n\n Status: Chartered company administration; Capital: Mombasa; Official languages: English; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Government: Commercial company rule; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 24 May 1887; Disestablished: 1 July 1895; Succeeded by: East Africa Protectorate

name: Anglo-French Joint Naval Commission
description: The Anglo-French Joint Naval Commission was created on 16 October 1887 as a bilateral condominium to maintain basic security and protect European residents across the New Hebrides archipelago. Lacking a settled administrative capital, the commission was staffed by naval officers from the British Royal Navy and the French Navy who periodically patrolled the islands aboard warships. The arrangement governed the archipelago until October 1906, when Great Britain and France established the permanent Anglo-French Condominium of the New Hebrides. \n\n Status: Condominium naval commission; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: English and French; Common languages: Bislama; Government: Joint naval administration; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 16 October 1887; Disestablished: 20 October 1906; Succeeded by: New Hebrides Condominium

name: Indochinese Union
description: The Indochinese Union was formed on 17 October 1887 as a grand administrative federation uniting the French protectorates of Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia alongside the direct colony of French Cochinchina. Administered successively from Saigon and Hanoi under a governor-general, the colonial union later incorporated Laos in 1899 and the leased territory of Guangzhouwan. The federation directed resource exploitation, railway construction and colonial commerce until Japanese wartime forces toppled French administration across Southeast Asia in 1941. \n\n Status: Federation of colonies and protectorates of France; Capital: Saigon and Hanoi; Official languages: French; Common languages: Vietnamese, Khmer, Lao and Cantonese; Government: Colonial governor-generalship; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 17 October 1887; Disestablished: 9 November 1953; Succeeded by: State of Vietnam, Kingdom of Cambodia and Kingdom of Laos

name: Kingdom of Alo
description: The Kingdom of Alo, historically known as Tu'a, was a traditional customary chiefdom situated on eastern Futuna and nearby Alofi in the South Pacific. Governed from the coastal village of Alo, the realm was led by a paramount king known as the Tu'i Agaifo, who ruled alongside Catholic Marist missionaries. On 29 November 1887, local chiefs signed a treaty accepting French protection, leading directly to the incorporation of Alo into the unified Wallis and Futuna Protectorate in March 1888. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Alo; Official languages: French; Common languages: Futunan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Customary Polynesian monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 29 November 1887; Disestablished: 5 March 1888; Succeeded by: Wallis and Futuna Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Sigave
description: The Kingdom of Sigave constituted a traditional Polynesian chiefdom occupying the western half of Futuna Island in the southwestern Pacific. Seated at the coastal settlement of Leava around Singave Bay, the polity was headed by a hereditary sovereign styled the Keletaona who governed under the close influence of Catholic missionaries. Following the protectorate treaty of 29 November 1887, Sigave retained its customary institutions while merging administratively into the overarching Wallis and Futuna Protectorate on 5 March 1888. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Leava; Official languages: French; Common languages: Futunan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Customary Polynesian monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 29 November 1887; Disestablished: 5 March 1888; Succeeded by: Wallis and Futuna Protectorate

name: Colony of Zululand
description: The Colony of Zululand was established as a British Crown possession in 1888 following the pacification and formal annexation of the defeated Zulu Kingdom. Administered from Eshowe by a British resident commissioner, the colonial authority subdivided traditional lands into native reserves and white settlement blocks while curtailing royal power. Following the suppression of Dinuzulu's rebellion in the late 1880s, the Crown integrated the territory into the neighbouring Colony of Natal in December 1897. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Eshowe; Official languages: English; Common languages: Zulu; Religion: Traditional Zulu religion and Christianity; Government: Colonial residency; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1888; Disestablished: 1898; Succeeded by: Colony of Natal

name: Rumaliza's Sultanate
label: arab polities of east congo
description: Rumaliza's Sultanate flourished around Lake Tanganyika in the late 1880s under the command of Omani-Swahili merchant Muhammad bin Khalfan bin Khamis al-Barwani, popularly known as Rumaliza. Operating from his fortified mercantile base at Ujiji, Rumaliza commanded a formidable personal army of Manyema warriors and maintained an extensive monopoly over regional ivory and slave routes. His commercial dominion collapsed in February 1894 when Belgian forces under Francis Dhanis captured his riverine strongholds during the Congo Arab War. \n\n Status: Sovereign mercantile sultanate; Capital: Ujiji; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Mercantile autocracy; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1888; Disestablished: 1 February 1894; Succeeded by: Congo Free State and German East Africa

name: Wallis and Futuna Protectorate
description: The Wallis and Futuna Protectorate was formed on 5 March 1888 when France unified the traditional island chiefdoms of 'Uvea, Alo and Sigave into a single colonial dependency. Governed from Mata-Utu under the overall administrative oversight of the governor of New Caledonia, the protectorate preserved the hereditary authority of indigenous customary kings alongside the French resident. This stable administrative structure persisted throughout the early twentieth century until the territory was reorganised into a French overseas collectivity. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Mata-Utu; Official languages: French; Common languages: Wallisian and Futunan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial protectorate; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 5 March 1888; Disestablished: 1925; Succeeded by: Overseas Territory of Wallis and Futuna

name: State of North Borneo
description: The State of North Borneo was formally recognised as a British protectorate on 12 May 1888, confirming the governing authority of the British North Borneo Chartered Company over modern Sabah. Administered from Sandakan, the chartered company developed timber logging, tobacco plantations and railway infrastructure while respecting local customary law among indigenous Dusun and Bajau communities. British protectorate administration endured until Imperial Japanese forces invaded the island in January 1942 during the Second World War. \n\n Status: Protected state of Great Britain; Capital: Sandakan; Official languages: English; Common languages: Kadazan-Dusun, Bajau, Malay and Chinese dialects; Government: Chartered company protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 12 May 1888; Disestablished: 19 January 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese occupation of British Borneo

name: Christmas Island
description: Christmas Island was formally annexed to the British Crown on 6 June 1888 following the discovery of extensive, high-grade phosphate deposits across the isolated Indian Ocean territory. Administered from Flying Fish Cove, the island was initially attached to the Straits Settlements, with the Christmas Island Phosphate Company recruiting Chinese and Malay labourers to conduct open-cast mining operations. British colonial oversight continued until March 1942, when Japanese military forces occupied the island to secure its mineral output. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Flying Fish Cove; Official languages: English; Common languages: Cantonese, Malay and Hokkien; Government: Colonial dependency; Historical era: Imperial expansion; Established: 6 June 1888; Disestablished: 1 April 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese occupation of Christmas Island

name: Sultanate of Pahang
description: The Sultanate of Pahang accepted British protection on 1 September 1888 after Sultan Ahmad al-Mu'azzam Shah signed a treaty consenting to the appointment of a British resident at Pekan. The residency system transformed local revenue collection, mining concessions and judicial administration while sparking armed resistance during the Pahang Uprising of the 1890s. In July 1896, British authorities merged Pahang with Perak, Selangor and Negeri Sembilan to create the Federated Malay States. \n\n Status: Protected state of Great Britain; Capital: Pekan; Official languages: Malay; Common languages: Pahang Malay and English; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate under British residency; Historical era: Imperial Malaya; Established: 1 September 1888; Disestablished: 1 July 1896; Succeeded by: Federated Malay States

name: Sultanate of Brunei
description: The Sultanate of Brunei became a British protectorate on 17 September 1888 when Sultan Hashim Jalilul Alam Aqamaddin concluded a treaty of protection to prevent further territorial dismemberment by neighbouring Sarawak and North Borneo. Governed from Bandar Seri Begawan, then known as Brunei Town, the rump sultanate surrendered control of its foreign affairs while preserving internal royal sovereignty under the ruling Bolkiah dynasty. The protectorate arrangement endured until Japanese forces invaded coastal Borneo in December 1941. \n\n Status: Protected state of Great Britain; Capital: Bandar Seri Begawan; Official languages: Malay; Common languages: Brunei Malay and English; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute Islamic monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Malaya; Established: 17 September 1888; Disestablished: 22 December 1941; Succeeded by: Japanese occupation of British Borneo

name: Gabon
description: Gabon was established as a distinct French colonial territory on 11 December 1888, following the administrative separation of coastal Gabonese settlements from the larger French Congo administration. Centred at Libreville on the Gabon Estuary, the colony served as an essential operational base for French commercial penetration and forestry concessions across Central Africa. Gabon underwent repeated administrative amalgamations within French Equatorial Africa before regaining separate territorial status and achieving complete independence in August 1960. \n\n Status: Colony of France; Capital: Libreville; Official languages: French; Common languages: Fang, Myene, Punu and Teke; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 11 December 1888; Disestablished: 17 August 1960; Succeeded by: Gabonese Republic

name: Colony of Trinidad and Tobago
description: The Colony of Trinidad and Tobago was formally unified under a single British colonial administration on 1 January 1889, joining the previously separate island dependencies into one Crown colony. Governed from Port of Spain, the amalgamated colony developed a vibrant multi-ethnic society shaped by European planters, Afro-Caribbean descendants and East Indian indentured labourers. The colony expanded cocoa production and petroleum extraction across the early twentieth century before securing full national independence within the Commonwealth in August 1962. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Port of Spain; Official languages: English; Common languages: Trinidadian English, Trinidadian Creole, Tobagonian Creole and Hindustani; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Modern colonial era; Established: 1889; Disestablished: 31 August 1962; Succeeded by: Trinidad and Tobago

name: Kingdom of Rarotonga
description: The Kingdom of Rarotonga was established as a British protectorate in 1889 when Queen Makea Takau Ariki and the island council formally requested imperial protection against feared French territorial expansion. Administered from Avarua on Rarotonga, the realm retained indigenous chiefly governance under the traditional Ariki council while British resident Frederick Moss advised on legislation and public finances. In 1893, the protectorate was reorganised into the Cook Islands Federation, which was later annexed to New Zealand. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Avarua; Official languages: Cook Islands Maori and English; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Customary constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 1889; Disestablished: 1894; Succeeded by: Cook Islands Federation

name: North Hsenwi State
label: shan states
description: North Hsenwi State was created in 1889 following the British partition of the ancient Hsenwi principality into two manageable administrative territories in the Northern Shan States. Centred on the historic capital of Hsenwi, with British administrative officers residing at Lashio, the state was ruled by a hereditary saopha presiding over Shan and Kachin populations. The principality flourished as a major hub for cross-border trade with Yunnan until Shan princely powers were integrated into independent Burma in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British protection; Capital: Hsenwi; Common languages: Shan, Kachin and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary saopha monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1889; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: South Hsenwi State
label: shan states
description: South Hsenwi State was established in 1889 when British colonial authorities separated the southern districts of the historic Hsenwi kingdom following the third Anglo-Burmese conflict. Headquartered at Mong Yai, the state was ruled by an autonomous saopha who oversaw rich agricultural valleys and upland trade routes. The principality maintained its internal dynastic administration under British supervision throughout the colonial era, acceding to the newly created Union of Burma upon the termination of British rule in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British protection; Capital: Mong Yai; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary saopha monarchy; Historical era: British Burma; Established: 1889; Disestablished: 4 January 1948; Succeeded by: Union of Burma

name: State of Sarawak
description: The State of Sarawak entered into a formal treaty of protection with Great Britain in 1889, confirming the international sovereignty and hereditary rule of the Brooke dynasty, known as the White Rajahs. Governed from the riverine capital of Kuching by Charles Brooke, the state prospered through timber concessions, pepper cultivation, oil extraction and rubber plantations. Sarawak retained extensive domestic autonomy under British imperial protection until the rapid advance of Imperial Japanese forces overwhelmed the country in April 1942. \n\n Status: Protected state of Great Britain; Capital: Kuching; Official languages: English and Malay; Common languages: Iban, Bidayuh, Melanau and Chinese dialects; Government: Hereditary constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Borneo; Established: 1889; Disestablished: 1 April 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese occupation of British Borneo

name: Sagallo
description: Sagallo was a short-lived Russian colonial and religious settlement founded on 6 January 1889 on the Gulf of Tadjoura in modern-day Djibouti by Cossack adventurer Nikolai Ivanovitch Achinov. Proclaiming an Orthodox colony dubbed New Moscow, the Russian expedition occupied an abandoned Egyptian fort without official diplomatic authorisation from Saint Petersburg. Viewing the settlement as an encroachment upon the French protectorate of Obock, a French naval squadron bombarded and seized the outpost on 5 February 1889, expelling the settlers. \n\n Status: Colonial settlement enclave; Capital: Sagallo; Official languages: Russian; Common languages: Afar and Somali; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Armed frontier settlement; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 6 January 1889; Disestablished: 5 February 1889; Succeeded by: French Somaliland

name: Italian Somaliland
description: Italian Somaliland took form on 8 February 1889 when the Kingdom of Italy concluded protectorate treaties with northern Somali rulers before establishing direct administrative enclaves along the Benadir coast. Governed from the historic maritime city of Mogadishu, the colonial regime expanded inland through military campaigns, agricultural concessions along the Shebelle River and corporate administration. In June 1936, Italian authorities consolidated Somaliland with conquered Ethiopian lands and Eritrea to establish the grand colonial framework of Italian East Africa. \n\n Status: Colony of the Kingdom of Italy; Capital: Mogadishu; Official languages: Italian; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 8 February 1889; Disestablished: 1 June 1936; Succeeded by: Italian East Africa

name: Sultanate of Hobyo
description: The Sultanate of Hobyo, also known as Obbia, became an Italian protectorate on 9 February 1889 when Sultan Yusuf Ali Kenadid signed a treaty granting Rome foreign policy control in exchange for annual subsidies. Governed from the central Somali coastal port of Hobyo, the sultanate commanded extensive livestock herds, coastal trade and desert caravans traversing the Mudug plateau. Italy utilised the protectorate as a strategic stepping stone for regional expansion before annexing Hobyo directly into Italian Somaliland in May 1889. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Kingdom of Italy; Capital: Hobyo; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 9 February 1889; Disestablished: 1 May 1889; Succeeded by: Italian Somaliland

name: Kingdom of Rimatara
description: The Kingdom of Rimatara was a traditional Polynesian monarchy on the westernmost inhabited island of the Austral archipelago in French Polynesia. Governed from the royal village of Amaru, the island community accepted French protectorate status on 29 March 1889 to ensure maritime security against foreign naval intervention. The indigenous Protestant monarchy maintained local customary administration under French naval supervision until 2 September 1901, when France formally annexed Rimatara into the French Settlements in Oceania. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Amaru; Common languages: Austral, Tahitian and French; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Customary Polynesian monarchy; Historical era: Imperial Pacific expansion; Established: 29 March 1889; Disestablished: 2 September 1901; Succeeded by: French Settlements in Oceania

name: African Lakes Company
description: The African Lakes Company was a Scottish chartered commercial enterprise founded to promote legitimate trade and counter Swahili slave caravans across modern Malawi. Operating from its principal commercial depot at Blantyre, the corporation managed steam navigation on Lake Malawi and the Shire River while opening trading stations and coffee plantations across the highlands. Escalating military clashes with Arab-Swahili trading warlords overwhelmed the company's private resources, prompting Great Britain to establish formal imperial protectorate authority over Nyasaland in 1892. \n\n Status: Chartered commercial corporation; Capital: Blantyre; Official languages: English; Common languages: Chewa, Tumbuka and Yao; Religion: Presbyterianism; Government: Commercial company administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1 April 1889; Disestablished: 1892; Succeeded by: British Central Africa Protectorate

name: Majeerteen Sultanate
description: The Majeerteen Sultanate, also known as the Migiurtinia Kingdom, entered into an imperial protection treaty with the Kingdom of Italy on 7 April 1889 under the leadership of Boqor Osman Mahamuud. Headquartered at the northern coastal anchorage of Alula, the sultanate maintained a powerful hereditary monarchy that directed prosperous frankincense harvesting and extensive Red Sea maritime commerce. Although designed to safeguard royal sovereignty, the treaty quickly facilitated expanding Italian colonial hegemony across the Horn of Africa, culminating in integration into Italian Somaliland. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Kingdom of Italy; Capital: Alula; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 7 April 1889; Disestablished: 1 May 1889; Succeeded by: Italian Somaliland

name: Colony of Ubangi-Shari
description: The Colony of Ubangi-Shari was founded on 10 May 1889 when French explorer Paul Crampel established a permanent military and trading post at Bangui along the northern bank of the Ubangi River. The territory served as the strategic springboard for French military penetration into the central African interior and the Lake Chad basin, despite severe indigenous resistance against concessionary rubber extraction companies. In 1910, the colony was incorporated into French Equatorial Africa, eventually securing independence in August 1960 as the Central African Republic. \n\n Status: Colony of France; Capital: Bangui; Official languages: French; Common languages: Sango, Gbaya and Banda; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 10 May 1889; Disestablished: 13 August 1960; Succeeded by: Central African Republic

name: Independent Commune of Franceville
description: The Independent Commune of Franceville was established on 9 August 1889 on Efate Island in the New Hebrides by European plantation owners seeking basic civil order under the neutral regime of the Anglo-French Joint Naval Commission. Centred on the settlement that later became Port Vila, the municipality drafted a progressive local constitution led by Ferdinand Chevillard, electing a mayor and council that granted voting rights irrespective of race or sex. The experimental settler commune dissolved in July 1890 when the joint naval commission resumed direct supervision over the islands. \n\n Status: Unrecognised settler municipality; Administrative seat: Franceville; Official languages: French and English; Common languages: Bislama; Government: Municipal elective council; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 9 August 1889; Disestablished: 1 July 1890; Succeeded by: Anglo-French Joint Naval Commission

name: Republic of the United States of Brazil
description: The Republic of the United States of Brazil was established on 15 November 1889 following a bloodless military coup led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca that deposed Emperor Pedro II. Governed from Rio de Janeiro under the 1891 federal constitution, the republic dismantled imperial centralisation in favour of extensive provincial autonomy dominated by wealthy coffee and dairy oligarchies in São Paulo and Minas Gerais. Known historically as the Old Republic, this political order expanded agrarian exports and national infrastructure until being toppled by the Revolution of 1930. \n\n Status: Federal presidential republic; Capital: Rio de Janeiro; Official languages: Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal presidential republic; Legislature: National Congress; Historical era: First Brazilian Republic; Established: 15 November 1889; Disestablished: 24 January 1967; Succeeded by: Federative Republic of Brazil

name: Katunga and Chiromo
description: Katunga and Chiromo comprised a temporary Portuguese military enclave situated at the confluence of the Ruo and Shire rivers in southern Malawi, established on 1 December 1889 during imperial border rivalries. Commanded by Major Alexandre de Serpa Pinto, Portuguese armed forces occupied the river landings to assert territorial claims linking Angola to Mozambique across the British sphere in the Zambezi basin. Confronted by the British Ultimatum of January 1890, the Portuguese government ordered the immediate withdrawal of its expeditionary forces on 12 March 1890, abandoning the positions to Great Britain. \n\n Status: Military occupation post; Capital: Chiromo; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Sena and Chewa; Government: Military garrison command; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1 December 1889; Disestablished: 12 March 1890; Succeeded by: British Central Africa Protectorate

name: British South Africa Company
description: The British South Africa Company was incorporated under royal charter by Cecil Rhodes in 1889 to spearhead British imperial expansion and mining development across south-central Africa. Administered from Salisbury, the company deployed the Pioneer Column to occupy Mashonaland and Matabeleland, establishing administrative control through armed conquest over what became Southern and Northern Rhodesia. Corporate governance presided over railway construction, mineral prospecting and settler farming until September 1923, when the Crown transformed the company's territories into self-governing colonies. \n\n Status: Chartered company administration; Capital: Salisbury; Official languages: English; Common languages: Shona, Northern Ndebele and Bemba; Government: Commercial company administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1890; Disestablished: 12 September 1923; Succeeded by: Southern Rhodesia and Northern Rhodesia

name: Italian Company for Somalia V. Filonardi and Company
description: The Italian Company for Somalia V. Filonardi and Company was a chartered commercial enterprise established to administer Italy's expanding colonial interests along the Benadir coast. Headed by diplomat Vincenzo Filonardi, the firm governed leased southern coastal ports including Mogadishu, Barawa and Merca under concessionary agreements with the Sultan of Zanzibar. Local resistance and financial difficulties hampered commercial exploitation, leading the Italian government to supersede company administration in 1897. \n\n Status: Chartered company administration under Italian suzerainty; Capital: Mogadishu; Common languages: Italian, Somali and Arabic; Religion: Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Corporate colonial administration; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1890; Disestablished: 1897; Succeeded by: Italian Commercial Company of Benadir

name: Jimma Abba Jifar
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: Jimma Abba Jifar was an autonomous Oromo monarchy situated in the fertile Gibe region of south-western Ethiopia. Under the diplomatic leadership of King Abba Jifar II, the kingdom accepted tributary vassalage beneath the Ethiopian Empire, thereby preserving its traditional governance, Islamic culture and commercial prosperity. The state maintained substantial internal independence until the centralising reforms of Emperor Haile Selassie prompted its formal absorption into the imperial provincial administration. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ethiopian Empire; Capital: Jiren; Common languages: Oromo and Amharic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional absolute monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1890; Disestablished: 1933; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Kingdom of Jimma
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Jimma was the most powerful Oromo state in the Gibe basin, positioned south of the Gojeb River in south-western Ethiopia. Having concluded an advantageous submission treaty with Emperor Menelik II, the realm operated as an autonomous imperial dependency renowned for its extensive coffee plantations and bustling trade routes. It retained its hereditary crown until the death of its longtime monarch in May 1932, whereupon imperial authorities dissolved its autonomous status. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ethiopian Empire; Capital: Jiren; Common languages: Oromo and Amharic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1890; Disestablished: 12 May 1932; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Kingdom of Rurutu
description: The Kingdom of Rurutu was an indigenous Polynesian island realm encompassing the northernmost elevated atoll of the Austral archipelago. Following decades of monarchical rule influenced by British Protestant missionaries, the island became a French protectorate in 1890 while retaining its local royal court at Moerai. This transitional arrangement endured until August 1900, when France formally annexed the island into the French Establishments in Oceania. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Moerai; Common languages: Austral, Tahitian and French; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Monarchy under colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1890; Disestablished: 25 August 1900; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: Phulra State
label: indian princely states
description: Phulra State was a minor Muslim princely principality situated in the rugged Hazara region of the North-West Frontier. Ruled by hereditary khans of the Pashtun Tanoli clan, the small state had originated as a semi-independent fief carved out from neighbouring Amb. Under British indirect rule, the rulers maintained internal civil authority until the post-independence integration of frontier states into the Dominion of Pakistan. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Phulra; Common languages: Hindko, Pashto and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary chiefdom; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1890; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Pakistan

name: Territory of Oklahoma
description: The Territory of Oklahoma was an organised incorporated possession of the United States formed from the western section of the Indian Territory and the public land strip known as No Man's Land. Governed from Guthrie under federal legislation, the territory expanded rapidly through successive land runs that opened indigenous treaty reservations to American homesteaders. In November 1907, the territorial administration ceased when Oklahoma united with the remaining Indian Territory to enter the Union as the forty-sixth state. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory of the United States; Capital: Guthrie; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and indigenous languages; Government: Territorial administration; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 2 May 1890; Disestablished: 16 November 1907; Succeeded by: Oklahoma

name: Sultanate of Witu
description: The Sultanate of Witu was a Swahili coastal realm situated inland from Lamu along the eastern shores of modern Kenya. Founded by refugees of the Nabahani dynasty of Pate, the state transferred from German oversight to British protection following the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of July 1890. Protracted armed confrontations with British expeditionary forces eroded its sovereignty, ultimately reducing the sultanate to an administrative dependency absorbed into the surrounding East Africa Protectorate. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Witu; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy under colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1 July 1890; Disestablished: 1906; Succeeded by: East Africa Protectorate

name: French Sudan
description: French Sudan was an expansive colonial territory established across the upper Niger and Senegal river basins in western Africa. Formed in August 1890 following military conquests of the Toucouleur and Wassoulou empires, the colony was administered from Bamako and formed an integral constituent of the Federation of French West Africa. In April 1959, the territory joined neighbouring Senegal to form the transient Mali Federation, leading to complete sovereignty the subsequent year. \n\n Status: Colony of France; Capital: Bamako; Official languages: French; Common languages: Bambara, Fula and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam and animism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 18 August 1890; Disestablished: 4 April 1959; Succeeded by: Mali Federation

name: Kingdom of Dahomey (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Dahomey under military occupation represents the transitional period during which French expeditionary forces subjugated the Fon monarchy on the Abomey plateau. Prompted by coastal trade rivalries and border clashes along the Ouémé River, French troops under Colonel Alfred Dodds captured the royal capital of Abomey in late 1892 and exiled King Béhanzin. French officers established martial oversight over the fragmented kingdom until formal civil administration was instituted under the Colony of Dahomey. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone under French command; Capital: Abomey; Common languages: Fon and French; Religion: Vodun and Roman Catholicism; Government: French military administration; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 4 October 1890; Disestablished: 1895; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Makrai State
label: indian princely states
description: Makrai State was a small princely domain located within the Nerbudda Division of the Central Provinces of British India. Governed by a hereditary Rajput dynasty bearing the title of Raja, the state formed an isolated territorial enclave surrounded by British-administered districts in the Mahadeo Hills. The principality preserved its local autonomy through a subsidiary relationship with the colonial government until acceding to the newly independent Dominion of India in January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Makrai; Common languages: Hindi and Gondi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1891; Disestablished: 2 January 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Protectorate of Northern Nigeria
description: The Protectorate of Northern Nigeria was a British colonial dependency that encompassed the vast savannas and historic emirates north of the Niger and Benue rivers. Administered from Zungeru by High Commissioner Frederick Lugard, the protectorate incorporated the subdued Sokoto Caliphate and the Kanem-Bornu territories under the pioneering administrative framework of indirect rule. In January 1914, the territory amalgamated with its southern counterpart to establish the unified Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Zungeru; Official languages: English; Common languages: Hausa, Fula, Kanuri and Nupe; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional faiths; Government: Colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1891; Disestablished: 1914; Succeeded by: Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria

name: Wukari Federation
description: The Wukari Federation was a traditional Jukun polity located in the fertile Benue River valley of central Nigeria. Serving as the principal successor state to the ancient Kwararafa confederacy, the federation was ruled by a sacred king styled the Aku Uka from his seat at Wukari. After entering into British protectorate agreements in 1891, the realm retained cultural and judicial influence while colonial officials integrated its territories into the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria. \n\n Status: Traditional state under British protectorate; Capital: Wukari; Common languages: Jukun, Hausa and English; Religion: Traditional Jukun religion and Christianity; Government: Sacred monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1891; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Protectorate of Northern Nigeria

name: Republic of Chile
description: The Republic of Chile between February and September 1891 denotes the constitutional presidential government led by José Manuel Balmaceda during the Chilean Civil War. Operating from the capital of Santiago, Balmaceda's administration commanded the regular army in defence of strong executive authority against the insurgent naval and congressional coalition. The conflict ended abruptly in September 1891 when congressional forces captured Valparaíso and Santiago, leading to the collapse of the presidential regime and Balmaceda's suicide. \n\n Status: Sovereign presidential republic; Capital: Santiago; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential constitutional republic; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1 February 1891; Disestablished: 18 September 1891; Succeeded by: Parliamentary Republic of Chile

name: Government Junta of Iquique
description: The Government Junta of Iquique was the revolutionary authority established by Chilean congressional deputies and naval officers during the 1891 civil war against President José Manuel Balmaceda. Operating from the northern port of Iquique, the junta was presided over by Captain Jorge Montt and funded by valuable regional nitrate revenues. After raising an effective army that defeated Balmaceda's loyalists in central Chile, the junta entered Santiago in September 1891 to inaugurate Chile's parliamentary republic era. \n\n Status: Revolutionary provisional government; Capital: Iquique; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional revolutionary junta; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 15 February 1891; Disestablished: 18 September 1891; Succeeded by: Parliamentary Republic of Chile

name: French Guinea
description: French Guinea was a colonial territory established along the Upper Guinea coast of West Africa, succeeding the earlier administrative division of Rivières du Sud. Governed from the coastal port of Conakry, the colony formed an constituent component of the Federation of French West Africa from 1895 onwards. In September 1958, Guinean voters overwhelmingly rejected Charles de Gaulle's proposed French Community, resulting in the declaration of full national sovereignty under President Ahmed Sékou Touré on 2 October 1958. \n\n Status: Colony of France; Capital: Conakry; Official languages: French; Common languages: Fula, Mandinka and Susu; Religion: Sunni Islam, animism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 17 December 1891; Disestablished: 2 October 1958; Succeeded by: Republic of Guinea

name: British Central Africa Protectorate
description: The British Central Africa Protectorate was a colonial territory established across the Shire Highlands and along the western shores of Lake Nyasa, covering the geography of present-day Malawi. Proclaimed to forestall Portuguese imperial expansion and protect Scottish Presbyterian missionary enterprises, the protectorate was administered from Zomba by Commissioner Harry Johnston. In July 1907, the colonial administration underwent formal restructuring when the territory was officially reconstituted and renamed the Nyasaland Protectorate. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Zomba; Official languages: English; Common languages: Chewa, Yao and Tumbuka; Religion: Christianity and traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1892; Disestablished: 6 July 1907; Succeeded by: Nyasaland Protectorate

name: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman
description: The Sultanate of Muscat and Oman was a maritime realm encompassing the south-eastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, governed by the hereditary Al Busaid dynasty. Following bilateral treaties concluded in 1891 and 1892, the state functioned as a British-protected monarchy while retaining nominal internal sovereignty over the coastline and desert interior. British military assistance repeatedly helped suppress tribal rebellions in the interior before a palace coup in 1970 modernised the polity into the Sultanate of Oman. \n\n Status: British protected state; Capital: Muscat; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Omani Arabic, Balochi and English; Religion: Ibadi Islam and Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1892; Disestablished: 9 August 1970; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Oman

name: Sultanate of Rafaï
description: The Sultanate of Rafaï was an Islamic realm established by the Zande people along the Chinko River in the eastern basin of the modern Central African Republic. In April 1892, Sultan Hetman entered into a treaty of alliance with King Leopold II, placing the state under the protectorate of the Congo Free State in exchange for firearms and territorial recognition. Belgian oversight terminated in February 1895 following border realignments that transferred the sultanate into the French colonial sphere. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Congo Free State; Capital: Rafai; Common languages: Zande, Banda and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional beliefs; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 8 April 1892; Disestablished: 9 February 1895; Succeeded by: French Congo

name: Niger Coast Protectorate
description: The Niger Coast Protectorate was a British administrative territory encompassing the maritime estuaries and river deltas of south-eastern Nigeria, originally established as the Oil Rivers Protectorate. Centred at Old Calabar, the administration was organised to secure British commercial monopolies over the lucrative palm oil trade and eliminate indigenous mercantile competition. In January 1900, the protectorate amalgamated with the chartered holdings of the Royal Niger Company to inaugurate the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Old Calabar; Official languages: English; Common languages: Efik, Igbo, Ibibio and Ijaw; Religion: Christianity and traditional faiths; Government: Colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 20 May 1892; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: Southern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Glorioso Islands
description: The Glorioso Islands comprise a low-lying coral archipelago situated in the northern Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and the Comoro Islands. Formally annexed by the French Navy in August 1892, the islands were initially exploited by private concessionaires who established coconut plantations and extracted guano deposits on Grande Glorieuse. French colonial authorities maintained administrative oversight until 1960, when the archipelago was reorganised as a district within the French Southern and Antarctic Lands. \n\n Status: Overseas possession of France; Administrative seat: Grande Glorieuse; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Malagasy; Government: Colonial island dependency; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 23 August 1892; Disestablished: 1 April 1960; Succeeded by: French Southern and Antarctic Lands

name: Emirate of Muri
label: fula jihads polities
description: The Emirate of Muri was a Fulani state established in the Benue River basin of eastern Nigeria as an offshoot of the Sokoto jihad. In 1892 and 1893, the reigning emir concluded protection treaties with the French naval explorer Louis Mizon, briefly establishing a French sphere of influence along the middle Benue. However, international diplomatic protests from Great Britain prompted France to repudiate Mizon's treaties in 1894, restoring the emirate to British imperial jurisdiction. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Administrative seat: Jalingo; Common languages: Fula and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Historical era: Scramble for Africa; Established: 1893; Disestablished: 1894; Succeeded by: Royal Niger Company

name: Hunza State
label: indian princely states
description: Hunza State was an ancient mountain principality located in the high Karakoram range of present-day northern Gilgit-Baltistan. Following the Anglo-Burusho War of 1891, the realm entered into a subsidiary alliance with the British Raj while acknowledging nominal suzerainty to Jammu and Kashmir. Governed from the historic fortress of Baltit by a hereditary ruler titled the Mir, the Burusho state preserved its internal autonomy until acceding to the newly created Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Baltit; Common languages: Burushaski, Wakhi, Shina and Persian; Religion: Ismaili Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary principality; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1893; Disestablished: 15 August 1947; Succeeded by: Pakistan

name: Sheikhdom of Bahrain
description: The Sheikhdom of Bahrain was an insular Arab realm in the Persian Gulf ruled by the Sunni Al Khalifa dynasty from the port city of Manama. Formalised under successive exclusive protection treaties with Great Britain, the sheikhdom surrendered control over foreign affairs and defence in exchange for imperial maritime security. Fuelled by its historical pearling industry and twentieth-century oil discoveries, Bahrain developed modern administrative institutions before terminating the treaty relationship to declare complete independence in August 1971. \n\n Status: British protected state; Capital: Manama; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Bahraini Arabic and English; Religion: Islam; Government: Hereditary sheikhdom; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1893; Disestablished: 15 August 1971; Succeeded by: State of Bahrain

name: Provisional Government of Hawaii
description: The Provisional Government of Hawaii was an interim administration established in Honolulu on 17 January 1893 following the armed overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani. Organised by the pro-annexation Committee of Safety under the leadership of Sanford B. Dole, the oligarchic regime exercised executive authority over the Hawaiian archipelago while lobbying for immediate incorporation into the United States. When American annexation stalled in Washington, the government drafted a new constitution, declaring the Republic of Hawaii in July 1894. \n\n Status: Provisional revolutionary government; Capital: Honolulu; Common languages: Hawaiian and English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Oligarchic provisional republic; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 17 January 1893; Disestablished: 4 July 1894; Preceded by: Kingdom of Hawaii; Succeeded by: Republic of Hawaii

name: Cook Islands Federation
description: The Cook Islands Federation was a British-administered colonial entity in the South Pacific comprising the southern and northern islands of the Cook archipelago. Formed after the Kingdom of Rarotonga integrated neighbouring island councils into a federal legislature under the guidance of British Resident Frederick Moss, the federation maintained internal governance from Avarua. This arrangement persisted until June 1901, when Britain formally transferred sovereignty and administration of the archipelago to the colony of New Zealand. \n\n Status: Colonial dependency of Great Britain; Capital: Avarua; Official languages: English and Cook Islands Maori; Religion: Protestant Christianity; Government: Federal parliamentary dependency; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1894; Disestablished: 1902; Preceded by: Kingdom of Rarotonga; Succeeded by: Cook Islands under New Zealand administration

name: Nagar State
label: indian princely states
description: Nagar State was a mountainous princely polity situated in the Karakoram highlands of northern Gilgit-Baltistan, opposite the neighbouring state of Hunza across the Hunza River. Governed by a hereditary Burusho ruler styled the Mir from the fortified capital of Nagar, the state entered into a subsidiary alliance with British India following the 1891 military campaign. While formally acknowledging the suzerainty of Jammu and Kashmir, Nagar retained internal judicial and domestic autonomy until acceding to Pakistan in 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Nagar; Common languages: Burushaski, Shina and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary principality; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1894; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Pakistan

name: Principality of Trinidad
description: The Principality of Trinidad was a self-proclaimed and unrecognised micronation declared over the uninhabited oceanic island of Trindade in the South Atlantic Ocean. Established in 1893 by the American-born adventurer James Harden-Hickey, who styled himself Prince James I, the claimed regime sought to construct an offshore military dictatorship and naval refuelling station. The micronational project collapsed completely in 1895 when British naval forces occupied the island, which was subsequently awarded to Brazilian sovereignty through international diplomacy. \n\n Status: Unrecognised self-proclaimed state; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English, French and Portuguese; Religion: Secular; Government: Self-proclaimed absolute monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 1894; Disestablished: 1 August 1895; Succeeded by: First Brazilian Republic

name: Donghak Rebels
description: The Donghak Rebels were an insurgent peasant movement that seized control of substantial portions of southern Korea during the Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894. Inspired by the indigenous Neo-Confucian religious tenets of Donghak and led by commander Jeon Bong-jun, the insurgents captured Jeonju Fortress and demanded sweeping land, social and anti-corruption reforms. Their armed resistance against Joseon royal troops prompted military interventions by both Qing China and Imperial Japan, which ultimately crushed the rebellion. \n\n Status: Insurgent revolutionary movement; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Korean; Religion: Donghak; Government: Peasant revolutionary council; Historical era: Late Joseon; Established: 25 March 1894; Disestablished: 1 April 1895; Succeeded by: Joseon Kingdom

name: Uganda Protectorate
description: The Uganda Protectorate was a British colonial dependency in East Africa established in June 1894 when the British Crown assumed territorial administration from the Imperial British East Africa Company. Centred administratively at Entebbe on Lake Victoria, the protectorate expanded outward from the core Kingdom of Buganda through successive treaties that incorporated Ankole, Toro and Bunyoro. The colonial regime maintained indirect rule through traditional monarchies until Uganda achieved full independence as a sovereign nation in October 1962. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Entebbe; Official languages: English; Common languages: Luganda, Swahili, Runyankore and Acholi; Religion: Christianity, Islam and traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial protectorate; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 18 June 1894; Disestablished: 9 October 1963; Succeeded by: Uganda

name: Republic of Hawaii
description: The Republic of Hawaii was a self-declared sovereign oligarchy established on 4 July 1894 to succeed the Provisional Government of Hawaii. Dominated by American-descended sugar planters and businessmen under President Sanford B. Dole, the republic governed the Hawaiian Islands while actively pursuing annexation to the United States. Following the outbreak of the Spanish-American War, the United States Congress approved the Newlands Resolution, formally annexing Hawaii as an unincorporated American territory on 12 August 1898. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Honolulu; Common languages: English and Hawaiian; Religion: Protestant Christianity; Government: Unitary oligarchic presidential republic; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 4 July 1894; Disestablished: 12 August 1898; Preceded by: Provisional Government of Hawaii; Succeeded by: Territory of Hawaii

name: National Coalition
description: The National Coalition was an insurgent civil and military alliance established during the Peruvian Civil War of 1894 to overthrow President Andrés Avelino Cáceres. Led by charismatic politician Nicolás de Piérola, the movement united civilian political factions and provincial guerrilla fighters known as montoneros to resist military authoritarianism. After months of rural campaigning across the Andes, coalition forces breached Lima in March 1895, securing Cáceres's resignation and initiating the civilian political era known as the Aristocratic Republic. \n\n Status: Insurgent revolutionary alliance; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Revolutionary provisional committee; Historical era: Late Modern; Established: 4 November 1894; Disestablished: 19 March 1895; Succeeded by: Republic of Peru

name: Ethiopia (Military Occupation)
description: Ethiopia under military occupation designates the various extraterritorial zones and security corridors held by the Ethiopian armed forces during regional conflicts in the Horn of Africa. These operations encompassed tactical buffer areas occupied during border conflicts with Somalia in the 1980s, occupied frontline sectors along the disputed Eritrean frontier between 1999 and 2000, and subsequent military deployments in central and southern Somalia from late 2006. These operational commands enforced military oversight pending international disengagements. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone under Ethiopian armed forces; Administrative seat: Mobile operational headquarters; Common languages: Amharic, Somali and Tigrinya; Religion: Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity and Sunni Islam; Government: Military command; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 September 1982; Reorganised: 25 December 2006

name: Japanese Concession in Tianjin
label: concessions in china
description: The Japanese Concession in Tianjin was an extraterritorial urban enclave granted to the Empire of Japan following the conclusion of the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895. Situated along the Hai River within the northern treaty port of Tianjin, the enclave was administered by a resident consul and an elected municipal council. It developed into a prominent commercial hub and strategic military staging ground for Japanese imperial expansion into northern China until its reversion at the end of World War II. \n\n Status: Treaty port concession of the Empire of Japan; Administrative seat: Consular municipal office; Common languages: Japanese and Mandarin Chinese; Government: Consular municipal administration; Historical era: Century of humiliation; Established: 17 April 1895; Disestablished: 15 October 1945; Succeeded by: Republic of China

name: Republic of Formosa
description: The Republic of Formosa was a short-lived self-proclaimed state established on the island of Taiwan by local gentry and Qing officials in May 1895. Formed to resist the island's cession to the Empire of Japan under the Treaty of Shimonoseki, the republic proclaimed its loyalty to Beijing while seeking foreign diplomatic protection. Despite stubborn resistance organised from Taipei and subsequently Tainan under commander Liu Yongfu, the fledgling republic collapsed in October 1895 as Japanese expeditionary forces captured the southern capital. \n\n Status: Unrecognised revolutionary state; Capital: Tainan; Common languages: Hokkien, Hakka, Mandarin and Formosan languages; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Constitutional republic; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 23 May 1895; Disestablished: 21 October 1895; Preceded by: Qing Taiwan; Succeeded by: Japanese Taiwan

name: East Africa Protectorate
description: The East Africa Protectorate was a British colonial territory encompassing roughly the geographical area of present-day Kenya, established in July 1895 after the insolvency of the Imperial British East Africa Company. Initially governed from the coastal port of Mombasa, the administrative centre transferred inland to Nairobi in 1905 following the construction of the strategic Uganda Railway. The territory witnessed substantial European white settlement and agricultural reorganisation before being reconstituted as Kenya Colony and Protectorate in June 1920. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Great Britain; Capital: Mombasa (1895 to 1905) and Nairobi (1905 to 1920); Official languages: English; Common languages: Swahili, Kikuyu, Luo and Kamba; Religion: Christianity, Islam and traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: New Imperialism; Established: 1 July 1895; Disestablished: 11 June 1920; Succeeded by: Kenya Colony and Protectorate

name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: The Sultanate of Zanzibar was an insular Swahili monarchy comprising Unguja and Pemba islands off the coast of East Africa, governed by the Arab Al Busaid dynasty. Following the establishment of a British protectorate, the sultanate was administered under close colonial supervision, punctuated by the brief Anglo-Zanzibar War of August 1896 when imperial warships bombarded the royal palace.
